newsitem.title: USA: Suicide group left multimedia archive on beliefs.
newsitem.headline: Suicide group left multimedia archive on beliefs.

text.p: The 39 people who committed suicide at a Californian mansion believed in a mix of Christianity, science fiction and apocalyptic millennialism, according to the multimedia archive they left behind.

"Planet Earth about to be recycled - Your only chance to survive or evacuate is to leave with us," says a transcript of an Oct. 5, 1996, videotape posted on the Heaven's Gate group's Web site on the Internet.
"Undercover 'Jesus' Surfaces Before Departure," reads the title of a statement dated Sept. 25, 1995, and posted on the colourful site crammed with Heaven's Gate writings.
In a section entitled "Our Position Against Suicide," the group, which ran an Internet services business, thought authorities might arrest them for their beliefs.

The legacy of the 39 men and women -- whose bodies were found on Wednesday at a $1.5 million mansion in exclusive Rancho Santa Fe near San Diego -- include videotapes, a book and the Web site packed with long theological treatises.

Authorities said Marshall Applewhite, identified as the group's charismatic leader, and his followers killed themselves believing a UFO hiding behind the Hale-Bopp comet now visible from Earth would take them to heaven.

Although the group burst into public consciousness with Wednesday's grim discovery, it had been active since the early 1970s, as a "UFO Cult" that received wide news coverage then. The group said it went into seclusion for 17 years before issuing a statement in 1988 and going public in 1992.

In various parts of the Web site, Applewhite outlined a theology in which extraterrestrials belonging to "the level above human" give selected humans "deposits" or "chips" that will enable them to attain heaven.

The site -- a collection of Web pages -- includes a drawing labeled "How a Member of the Kingdom of Heaven might appear" and showing a space alien similar to popular depictions of imagined extraterrestrials. The site sports many pictures of comets, nebulae and other astronomical phenomena.

Applewhite said Jesus Christ was selected by one of these space aliens -- dubbed "a member of the Kingdom of Heaven" -- and that the alien took over the physical body of Jesus around the time of Jesus's baptism by John the Baptist.
Applewhite, citing the Bible in his writings, believed Jesus then had the task of showing the way to membership of heaven.
"... Only those individuals who had received a 'deposit' containing a soul's beginning had the capacity to believe or recognise the Kingdom of Heaven's Representative," he continued.
"I am in the same position to today's society as was the One that was in Jesus then," wrote Applewhite, repeatedly referring to events 2,000 years ago.
Applewhite said he and a "task partner" in the early 1970s "incarnated into (moved into and took over) two human bodies that were in their forties."

Applewhite said his partner, "Ti," was his "heavenly Father" who created him but that Ti "returned to the Heavens in 1985." News reports said Ti was a nurse named Bonnie Nettles he met while in a hospital in the 1970s, who later died.
Applewhite said humans' greatest enemy were "Luciferians": other "space races" who are essentially fallen angels. He attacked sceptics as being subject to "Luciferian programming."

The suicide discussion mentions the 73 A.D. mass suicide by Jewish Zealots rebelling against Roman rule at a fortress in Masada, Israel. It raises the possibility that because of Heaven's Gate's position, authorities might try to arrest members or subject them to "psychological or physical torture."

The group referred to the 1992 federal siege on the cabin of Randall Weaver in Idaho's Ruby Ridge area, in which three people died, and the 1993 Waco siege in which more than 80 members of the Branch Davidian cult died following a 51-day stand-off with federal agents.
